By Jonathan Thatcher

Record levels on Wall Street have not yet marked the end of the boom in U.S. share prices, and near-term propoects for Japanese equities are looking good because of the weaker yen, UK-based fund managers said.
However, fund managers were more divided over the outlook for U.S. bonds, according to a monthly poll of managers by Reuters.
"The bull market (in U.S. shares) is not over," said BZW's Michael Hughes.
"What we have seen is that economic growth was a temporary spurt. There have been signs that activity is moderating," said Matthew Merritt, global strategist at ING Barings.
With little chance of an early Federal Reserve monetary tightening, there is still upside potential for stocks even though the market index last week surged past the 7,000-mark for the first time.
However, a number of fund managers were still keeping fairly underweight in U.S. stocks.
The poll showed they were putting 26 percent of their global equity allocations into North America, compared to 28 percent in January.
Eventually, the slower U.S. economy will cap corporate earnings there, Merritt said.
But in Japan, the yen's decline is painting a rosier picture for stocks. Fund managers hope the lower currency will boost Japanese exports and stave off challenges from other economies in the region.
Jason Collins at Skandia Life said his company's fund managers were very positive on Japan, and Hughes said he was looking to increase exposure to the Japanese market.
But for the moment, fund managers were generally sticking to current positions.
Merritt said he preferred to wait a little longer for Japanese authorities to tighten fiscal measures in the second quarter.
Elsewhere in Asia, South Korea, already out of favour because of labour troubles, will face increasing competition from Japanese exporters as the yen weakens.
But with the exception of South Korea and troubled Thailand, the rest of Asia is looking good, one fund manager said.
Allocations to Asia, excluding Japan, for February show a slight increase.
In bonds, some managers were getting a little nervous about the strength of the rally in U.S. Treasuries, but not enough to pull out of the market just yet.
The percentage allocated to U.S. bonds this month rose to almost 35 percent from January's 30.4 percent.
In Europe, the bulk of interest remained in Germany.
One fund manager said that apart from high yield European bonds, he saw little point in putting money in anything but the German market.
